runs.text: declares a new type whose only values are the

of the list. Each member is written with the type's name, a dot and its name. A variable of that type can only hold one of those members, so there are no invented values and no typos that go unnoticed.

blocks.title: A named traffic light
blocks.source:
Enum Semaforo
  Rojo, Amarillo, Verde
EndEnum
Algorithm Cruce
  Define luz As Semaforo <- Semaforo.Verde;
  If luz = Semaforo.Verde Then
    Write "Cruzar con ", luz;
  EndIf
EndAlgorithm

blocks.description: A box with the type Semaforo and its three members: Rojo, Amarillo and Verde. A variable luz, outside the box, points to the member Verde.

caption.text: An enumeration is a closed list. A variable of the type can only point to one of its members.

entries.text: Each member has an internal 32-bit ordinal from 0, in declaration order, but the program cannot convert it to a number.
An enumeration may be empty or have a single member.

blocks.title: A colour that does not exist
blocks.source:
Enum Semaforo
  Rojo, Amarillo, Verde
EndEnum
Algorithm Azul
  Define luz As Semaforo <- Semaforo.Azul;
EndAlgorithm

diagnostics.message: The enumeration has no member Azul

blocks.title: Comparing with less than
blocks.source:
Enum Semaforo
  Rojo, Amarillo, Verde
EndEnum
Algorithm OrdenEnum
  Write Semaforo.Rojo < Semaforo.Verde;
EndAlgorithm

runs.text: When running, a member is just its ordinal: a small integer in a slot. The name is recovered from the declaration when it needs to be written. Comparing two members means comparing two integers.

points.text: An enumeration is a type with a closed list of members.
They only accept equality and inequality.
